5 Questions For Libertarians Who Support Privatizing Marriage

This is actually really interesting. I hadn't thought about it this way before. It does make sense that having one law governing the defined parameters of millions of contracts requires less government than all of those individual contracts. This should be obvious, but it wasn't to me until I read this. Huh.

I think it could be argued that getting government out of the marriage business also means it would have to get out of the business of child custody, dissolutions and so on. A private industry would arise around the need rather than rely on government to sort it out.

Some of the argumentation made in the article is erroneous anyhow, such as the idea that biological parents would no longer be presumed to have custody over their own children. Do unwed parents now face this issue? It doesn't seem to be, not any more than we'd expect if the state stopped issuing marriage licenses to "certify" unions.

The author ends by asking: "Please explain how abolishing state-recognized marriage protects the family and helps insulate individuals from an increasingly Leviathan state."

This presumes there is no power in be able to define what constitutes a marriage. If people, rather than the state, are able to make that determination, it insulates individuals by permitting them to construct families as they, and not the state, see fit. That's all the explanation required to satisfy her demand.

I definitely hear you. And those are points the article didn't give proper consideration to. I believe in incremental change toward libertarian ideals. In the short term, I don't think marriage privatization is realistic, even if it is ideal in the long run. Also, marriage privatization should be pretty low on our priority list compared to all of the more immediate ways we can reduce the size of government and cut spending and waste. I think we should keep our sights on the one two punch of cutting government and simplifying the tax code/cutting taxes.

It does make sense that having one law governing the defined parameters of millions of contracts requires less government than all of those individual contracts.

I don't see how that makes any kind of sense at all. One size fits all government contracts with the associated need for their phonebooks full of regulation are exactly what libertarianism is against.

I don't support privatizing marriage. I support abolishing marriage as an institution all together. If people want to get married they should be able to define what that means to them. If that means entering a financial agreement that the government enforces then so be it. If that means coming to an agreement about raising children together then so be it. All of these things can exist without calling it marriage and without forcing everyone to define their marriage in the same way. Marriage is an agreement between two people in love, it should only be defined by those two people ( or 3 or 4 people i guess that's fine too).

I don't get the article at all, like I can't make heads or tail of any point being valid.

point by point -

  1. Begging the question. Who says need state recognition of relationships? we don't.

  2. Child custody - marriage isn't relevant, we already have system for that thru birth certificates and adoption processes. (if you want to fix that, let's add mandatory paternity testing) either way not related to marriage itself.

  3. spousal immunity. why is this even a good thing. drop it.

  4. ad hominem and requires the government recognition from point 1, which isn't necessary.

  5. I have no idea what this mean. how is marriage a buffer from the state? someone help me here.

Spousal immunity should not be abolished, but universalized. Nobody should be forced to testify. Spousal immunity only ever mitigated an injustice. The solution is to abolish the injustice (coerced testimony).

The questions are non-applicable, as I do not think it should be replaced by contract law. It should be replaced by automatic extension of civil rights and liberties afforded to married couples with zero governmental authority to say no or refuse to recognize private relationships for any reason. People say they're together, they're together. Period. People say they're not together, they're not together. Period. People have a dispute over custody of children... Well, that's a matter for sensible arbitration and you don't need arbitrary legal nonsense hinging on marriage recognition in order to handle it correctly. Divorce? Civil courts handle divorce. They also handle property disputes and lawsuits. If people entangle their assets, break up and have a dispute over who gets possession of what then you can arbitrate that without governmental marriage regulations too. If your ex won't give your car back, sue for it just like you'd sue in a divorce. A couple really wants to ensure legal claims over ownership shares in joint property? Start a damn LLC and take a 50-50 stake in company, or if you prefer, family holdings, assets and shares.

That bullshit pseudo-counter is like saying the government needs the power to selectively authorize free speech in order to leave it alone. Because the government needs the power to arrest you for speaking out when they dislike it in order to respect your right to speak out. Just like the government needs the power to arrest or otherwise punish you for marriages it dislikes in order to leave your marriage alone. Fuck that noise.

You know what a gay marriage ban is? That's government exercising it's right to selectively recognize marriage on it's own terms. Criminal and civil bigamy penalties leveled against people that are in willing plural marriages? Again, government exercising it's right to selectively recognize marriage on it's own terms. Ever-so-popular interracial marriage bans in the dustbin of history? Again, government exercising it's right to selectively recognize marriage on it's own terms. Every civil rights victory for marriage consists of reduced governmental authority to dictate the terms by which it may or may not recognize marriage. Total removal of governmental power to regulate marriage is the natural end-state of that struggle.

This all seems to boil down to "If we don't let the government control who gets married then they'll interfere in the lives of married couples as much as they do in everyone else's." To which the obvious answer is "so stop interfering period."
